title: Switching solvers: HiGHS, SCIP, CP-SAT, GLOP, Gurobi

blocks.text: 4.2.3 Switching Solvers: HiGHS, SCIP, CP-SAT, GLOP, Gurobi

GridCap's planning service runs the selection model on HiGHS. A colleague asks for a second opinion from SCIP before a board meeting, finance wants the LP budget prices from GLOP, and the vendor evaluation needs a Gurobi run. With MathOpt that is the same model handed to four solvers, and the code change is one argument. What changes with the solver is everything around that argument: which models it accepts, what it returns, and how much of its answer you can trust.

This lesson hands one GridCap model to every solver OR-Tools 9.15 ships, as an LP and as a MILP, and reads what comes back. The solver names follow MathOpt's `SolverType`: `GLOP` (Google's simplex LP solver), `PDLP` (Google's first-order LP solver, lesson 2.4.1), `HIGHS` (the open-source LP and MIP solver this course uses by default), `GSCIP` (SCIP, an open-source MIP solver, through Google's wrapper) and `CP_SAT` (Google's constraint-programming solver over integers, taught from lesson 4.4.1). GridCap is a fictional portfolio.
The Model
Both models are GridCap small's project-selection model of lesson 4.2.1.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the candidate projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$.
**Parameters.** $`v_i`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ at its earliest start ($k, an integer); $`c_{i,y}`$, what it spends in year $`y`$ ($k, an integer); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** MILP: $`x_i \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$. LP relaxation: $`0 \le x_i \le 1`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} v_i\, x_i
**Constraints.**
The rows are named `must_P002`, `alt_G006`, `needs_P004` and `budget_2027` in `selection.py`.
The Solver Is an Argument to solve, Never Part of the Model
`selection.build` returns a model that names no solver. The program builds both versions once and hands each to all five solvers, catching the solves that are refused:

small = generate("small")
models = {"LP": build(small, integer=False), "MILP": build(small)}


def attempt(kind: str, solver: mathopt.SolverType) -> str:
    sel = models[kind]
    try:
        result = solve(sel.model, solver)
    except Exception as error:          # a refusal; lesson 4.2.4 reads its message properly
        return "refused: " + str(error.__context__ or error).split(" [")[0]
    funded = plan(sel, result)
    extras = [name for name, has in (("duals", result.has_dual_feasible_solution()),
                                      ("basis", result.has_basis())) if has]
    count = f"  funded {len(funded)}" if kind == "MILP" else ""
    return (f"{result.termination.reason.name} {result.objective_value():,.1f}"
            f"{count}  {' + '.join(extras) or 'no duals'}")


for kind in models:
    print(kind)
    for solver in (S.GLOP, S.PDLP, S.HIGHS, S.GSCIP, S.CP_SAT):
        print(f"  {solver.name:<7} {attempt(kind, solver)}")

LP
  GLOP    OPTIMAL 23,669.5  duals + basis
  PDLP    OPTIMAL 23,669.5  duals
  HIGHS   OPTIMAL 23,669.5  duals + basis
  GSCIP   OPTIMAL 23,669.5  no duals
  CP_SAT  OPTIMAL 22,532.0  no duals
MILP
  GLOP    refused: Glop does not support integer variables
  PDLP    refused: PDLP does not support integer variables
  HIGHS   OPTIMAL 22,532.0  funded 25  no duals
  GSCIP   OPTIMAL 22,532.0  funded 25  no duals
  CP_SAT  OPTIMAL 22,532.0  funded 25  no duals
the three MILP solvers fund the same projects: True

The `solve` here is `selection.solve`, which calls `mathopt.solve` and keeps the bundled HiGHS's stray output off the screen (lesson 4.2.1). The solver went in as a value, `S.GLOP` through `S.CP_SAT`, and nothing else in the program changed. Several OR-Tools samples (`time_indexed_scheduling.py`, `facility_location.py`, `writing_seminar.py`) do the same at the command line: their solver is a flag whose type is `SolverType`, so a run can switch solvers without an edit. That is the pattern to copy: the model builder knows nothing of solvers, and the solver is configuration.
The grid answers four questions about the solvers, one per section below: which model types each accepts, what each returns, where CP-SAT's answer goes wrong, and which solvers you can use at all.
Each Solver Accepts Only the Model Types It Can Solve, and Says So Before Solving

The MILP column shows the first rule: **GLOP and PDLP solve LPs only**, and refuse a model with an integer variable. The refusal is an exception from `mathopt.solve`, raised before any work, never a status; in OR-Tools 9.15 its message is hidden on the exception's `__context__` (lesson 4.2.4). It is a good refusal: it stops you from getting an LP answer to a yes/no question.

The LP column shows the second: **only some solvers return dual values.** GLOP and HiGHS return duals and a basis (both use simplex); PDLP returns duals but no basis (it does not use simplex); SCIP solves the LP and returns no duals at all. The `SolverType` docstring says it plainly for SCIP: no dual data for LPs, prefer GLOP. So "read the budget's shadow price" (lesson 4.2.2) is a job for GLOP or HiGHS, and a program that switches solver must check `has_dual_feasible_solution()` rather than assume.

The three MILP solvers agree: the same value, $22,532k, and the same 25 projects. Agreement on a small model is a cheap and strong test of a model; when a solver change moves the objective, the first suspects are a tolerance (lesson 2.4.1) and a model feature one solver reads differently, which is what CP-SAT does in the LP column.
What each solver takes, from the `SolverType` docstrings and the runs above:

rows: yes, all variables integer and bounded

blocks.text: CP-SAT Needs Integers, and Rounds a Continuous Model Without Warning

The LP column's last line is wrong. CP-SAT reported `OPTIMAL 22,532.0` for the LP relaxation, whose optimum the other four agree is $23,669.5k. It solved a different model. CP-SAT works over integers only; the CP-SAT page of the OR-Tools documentation says to scale any non-integer terms to integers before using it, and MathOpt's `SolverType` docstring calls its handling of continuous variables experimental support to "rescale and discretize". The program shows what that did here:

lp = build(generate("small"), integer=False)          # every x[i] continuous in [0, 1]
for solver in (S.GLOP, S.HIGHS, S.CP_SAT):
    result = solve(lp.model, solver)
    fractional = sum(1 for v in lp.x.values() if 1e-6 < result.variable_values(v) < 1 - 1e-6)
    print(f"{solver.name:<6} {result.termination.reason.name} {result.objective_value():,.1f}"
          f"  fractional x: {fractional}")

GLOP   OPTIMAL 23,669.5  fractional x: 4
HIGHS  OPTIMAL 23,669.5  fractional x: 4
CP_SAT OPTIMAL 22,532.0  fractional x: 0

The LP's optimum funds four projects in part. CP-SAT returned no fractions at all: every $`x_i`$ came back 0 or 1, so it answered the MILP, and called that the optimum of the LP. A model with one continuous variable shows the same thing on a smaller scale:

model = mathopt.Model(name="one-continuous")
a = model.add_variable(lb=0, ub=10, name="a")              # continuous
b = model.add_integer_variable(lb=0, ub=10, name="b")
model.add_linear_constraint(0.37 * a + 1.13 * b <= 7.71, name="cap")
model.maximize(1.01 * a + 2.9 * b)
for solver in (S.HIGHS, S.CP_SAT):
    result = solve(model, solver)
    print(f"{solver.name:<6} {result.termination.reason.name} {result.objective_value():.4f}"
          f"  a = {result.variable_values(a):.4f}  b = {result.variable_values(b):g}")

HIGHS  OPTIMAL 20.3078  a = 8.6216  b = 4
CP_SAT OPTIMAL 19.6800  a = 8.0000  b = 4

HiGHS sets the continuous `a` to 8.6216, where the `cap` row is tight. CP-SAT stopped at `a = 8`, a whole number, and still said `OPTIMAL`. Its value is a feasible plan, so nothing breaks; it is just not the optimum of the model you wrote, and no field of the result says so. The rule that follows: **hand CP-SAT only models whose variables are all integer**, with integer data where you can (GridCap's money is in whole $k for that reason), and send anything with a continuous variable to HiGHS or SCIP. Lessons 4.4.1 to 4.4.4 teach CP-SAT in its own API, where integers are the only kind of variable.

Five Solvers Are Built Into the pip Package, and Gurobi Needs Its Own Library and License
`SolverType` lists more solvers than the OR-Tools wheel contains. Asking for each one shows which are there:

compiled into this OR-Tools:
  GSCIP     yes
  GLOP      yes
  CP_SAT    yes
  PDLP      yes
  GLPK      no: solver type SOLVER_TYPE_GLPK is not registered
  OSQP      no: solver type SOLVER_TYPE_OSQP is not registered
  ECOS      no: solver type SOLVER_TYPE_ECOS is not registered
  SCS       no: solver type SOLVER_TYPE_SCS is not registered
  HIGHS     yes
  SANTORINI no: solver type SOLVER_TYPE_SANTORINI is not registered

SCIP, GLOP, CP-SAT, PDLP and HiGHS are compiled in. GLPK, OSQP, ECOS, SCS and Santorini have a `SolverType` but no code behind it in this build: the full message adds that support for the solver has not been compiled, so naming one is refused at once.

Gurobi is the fifth kind: a commercial solver whose code is not in OR-Tools at all. MathOpt loads Gurobi's own shared library at run time, and Gurobi then needs a license. Here is what the course runner does with `SolverType.GUROBI`:

model = mathopt.Model(name="tiny")
x = model.add_binary_variable(name="x")
model.maximize(x)
try:
    result = mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.GUROBI)
    print("GUROBI:", result.termination.reason.name)
except Exception as error:
    print("GUROBI raised", type(error).__name__ + ":", error)
    print("hidden reason:", error.__context__)

GUROBI raised RuntimeError: bad_function_call
hidden reason: None

**Gurobi through MathOpt does not run in the course runner, so this page shows no Gurobi results.** The call fails with a C++ `bad_function_call`, which names no cause. The runner does have the `gurobipy` package (section 5 uses it directly), and that wheel ships a Gurobi library, so the program then points OR-Tools at it, in a child process because a failure there stops the process:

library = sorted((pathlib.Path(gurobipy.__file__).parent / ".libs").glob("libgurobi*.so"))[0]
probe = ("from ortools.init.python import init; "
         f"print('loaded', init.CppBridge.load_gurobi_shared_library({str(library)!r}))")
child = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", probe], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("gurobipy", ".".join(map(str, gurobipy.gurobi.version())), "ships", library.name)
print("loading it: exit code", child.returncode)
for line in child.stderr.splitlines():
    if "could not find function" in line:
        print("  ", line.split("] ", 1)[1].replace(str(library), library.name))

gurobipy 13.0.3 ships libgurobi130.so
loading it: exit code -6
   Check failed: function_address Error: could not find function GRBcopyparams in libgurobi130.so

OR-Tools 9.15 expects a function, `GRBcopyparams`, that the Gurobi 13 library does not have, and the child process aborted (exit code $`-6`$ is the abort signal). So in this course's pinned versions, Gurobi is used through `gurobipy` itself (section 5, from lesson 5.3.1). On a machine with a Gurobi version and license that OR-Tools supports, the same `mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.GUROBI)` call is all it takes; the model does not change. Never put a license file in a repository or an image; mount it at run time (lesson 5.3.4, in section 5).

Summary

items: **The solver is an argument to `solve`, never part of the model.** Build once, solve with any `SolverType`, and make the solver configuration.
**Each solver accepts only the model types it can solve.** GLOP and PDLP refuse integer variables, with an exception raised before solving.
**Only GLOP, HiGHS and PDLP return LP duals**; SCIP and CP-SAT do not, and no solver returns duals for a MILP.
**CP-SAT needs integers.** Handed a continuous variable, it rounds it and still reports `OPTIMAL`; give it all-integer models only.
**Five solvers are compiled into the pip package:** GLOP, PDLP, HiGHS, SCIP, CP-SAT. Gurobi needs its own library and license, and does not run through MathOpt in the course runner.

blocks.text: Reference

**Further reading:** [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (the solvers MathOpt can drive, and the note that Gurobi and Xpress need licenses); [MathOpt `parameters.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/parameters.py) (the `SolverType` docstrings: what each solver supports, SCIP's missing LP duals, CP-SAT's experimental discretizing); [MathOpt `parameters.proto`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/parameters.proto) (the same list at the protocol level, which already names Xpress); [CP-SAT Solver (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver) (CP-SAT works over integers only, and non-integer terms must be scaled first); [Advanced LP Solving (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/lp/lp_advanced) (GLOP's primal and dual simplex, and when to try PDLP or a commercial solver); [MathOpt sample time_indexed_scheduling.py](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/time_indexed_scheduling.py) (a solver taken as a `SolverType` flag, with SCIP as its default).
Challenges

items: Scale the one-continuous model so CP-SAT gets it right: replace `a` by an integer number of hundredths. What changes in the coefficients?
Solve GridCap medium with HiGHS, SCIP and CP-SAT. Do they fund the same projects? If not, are the objective values still equal?
Write the shortest program that tells a colleague whether MathOpt can use Gurobi on their machine, without printing anything that identifies the machine.

blocks.text: Design Note: Test a Model on Two Solvers

Switching solver costs one argument, so use it in tests. A test that solves a small instance with HiGHS and with SCIP and asserts the objective values agree (within a tolerance, lesson 2.4.1) catches two kinds of bug at once: a model that a solver reads differently than you intended (the CP-SAT case above) and a solver bug in a new release. It does not catch a model that is wrong in the same way for every solver; that needs hand-built feasible and infeasible plans, as the course's modeling practices use. Section 12 builds both kinds of test into the planning service.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**solver_grid.py.** GridCap small as an LP and as a MILP on GLOP, PDLP, HiGHS, SCIP and CP-SAT, and the list of solvers compiled into the wheel (*The Solver Is an Argument*, *Each Solver Accepts Only*, *Five Solvers Are Built Into the pip Package*). *Try:* Add the tiny portfolio as a third model. Predict which cells change.

**cpsat_continuous.py.** CP-SAT on a continuous model: the LP relaxation and a model with one continuous variable (*CP-SAT Needs Integers*). *Try:* Make `a` an integer variable. Predict both solvers' answers.

**gurobi_attempt.py.** What `SolverType.GUROBI` does in the course runner, and what happens when OR-Tools is pointed at the library inside `gurobipy` (*Gurobi Needs Its Own Library and License*). *Try:* Run it on a machine with Gurobi installed. Predict the termination reason.
